I woke up before the alarm this morning, which never happens, and lay there listening to the house settle into itself. Outside, a garbage truck was sighing down the street, and a dog barked twice and then thought better of it. The light coming through the blinds was that pale, uncertain gray that makes everything look like a photograph of itself. I did not get up right away, because there was no reason to, and that felt like a small victory all on its own. Some days you win by simply refusing to hurry. I let the quiet win anyway.

When I finally did get up, the kitchen was cold and the kettle took its time, as kettles do, unconcerned with my plans. I stood in my socks and watched the water climb into a shiver, and I thought about how many mornings I have watched exactly this and still found it interesting. There is a comfort in repetition that does not ask you to be impressed, only to be present. I made tea and stood by the window and watched the neighbors begin their day without me, which was a relief. No one needed anything from me yet today.

I have been thinking lately about the way we talk about time when we are not really talking about time at all. We say we are running out of it, as if it were something stored in a pantry, or that we are killing it, as if it were an insect under a glass. Both phrases feel wrong in a way I cannot quite name, but they feel wrong because time is not a thing we use. It is more like weather, or a river we are floating in, whether we paddle or not. We notice it when it changes.

Yesterday I took a walk not to exercise and not to get anywhere, which is harder than it sounds because my feet keep wanting to be efficient. I ended up on a street I have lived near for ten years and never actually walked down, which tells you something about how we live. The houses were ordinary in the way that somehow becomes singular if you look long enough. One had a porch swing painted blue, another had a garden that had clearly been abandoned to the mercy of the weeds. A cat watched me from a fence, entirely unimpressed.

I think we underestimate how much of a life is made of watching cats on fences, metaphorically speaking. Not the adventures, which are few, and not the big decisions, which feel big mostly in retrospect, but the long stretches of ordinary attention. Attention is a kind of love that does not require applause. It just says, I was here, I noticed, this mattered enough to stay a minute longer than necessary. I have been trying to practice that, on walks and in kitchens and in conversations where I would rather be planning my next sentence. It is difficult work indeed.

There is a drawer in my desk that I have not opened in maybe three years, and I think about it more than I open it. Inside are letters I never sent, a train ticket to a city I never visited, and a photograph I have never quite decided whether to keep or throw away. Every so often I tell myself I will sort through it on a rainy Sunday, which is my way of saying never. Perhaps that is the point, that some drawers are not for sorting but for remembering that you once meant to. Keep them forever.

I have a plant on my windowsill that I bought because it looked sad in the store and I felt, irrationally, responsible for it. It has not thrived, exactly, but it has persisted, which in plant terms and maybe in human terms counts for something. I water it when I remember, which is not often enough, and I talk to it when I am thinking aloud, which is often enough. Last week a new leaf appeared, small and bright and entirely unexpected, and I felt disproportionately proud, as if I had done something clever. It was just persistence, finally rewarded.

People keep telling me I should journal, as if a life without a written record is a life that evaporates. I do not doubt the value of writing things down, I only doubt that evaporation is such a bad thing. Some mornings should not be preserved in amber; they should be allowed to be exactly what they were, brief and forgotten. Forgetting is not failure, it is how the mind makes room for the next cat on the next fence. What I keep instead are small, useless facts, like the way light falls at four in the afternoon in November.

I am old enough now to have friends who live far away, and we sustain the friendship with voice notes that begin with, sorry this is long. We listen to them on walks or while washing dishes, and we deliberately do not respond immediately, because urgency would ruin the whole gentle arrangement. It is a strange, modern kind of letter, half confession and half weather report, sent into the ether with no expectation of an answer today. I like that it gives us permission to be rambling and unedited, which is rare enough to feel like a gift indeed. Anyway.

If you have read this far, you know what I know, which is that there is not much to conclude, only to continue. The kettle will boil again tomorrow, and the plant will need water eventually, and the drawer will stay closed a while longer. And I will probably wake up before the alarm again someday, and be surprised by it all over again, as if it were the first time. That is not a bad way to live, if you think about it, to be surprised by the ordinary until the very end. Thank you for staying with me.
